justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modestly upward-sloping baseline from current levels, with the 1-day estimate anchored closely to the last observed price and each subsequent horizon nudged slightly higher. The 1-day estimate of 326 is essentially a near-mean-reversion assumption — absent any overnight catalyst, prices tend to drift close to their recent closing level. The 1-week estimate of 328 incorporates a small positive drift consistent with the broader trend in whatever underlying asset this represents, while the 1-month estimate of 332 extends that drift further but with diminishing conviction, as longer horizons are increasingly influenced by macro factors and mean-reversion forces that are hard to predict with precision.

The confidence interval widths were calibrated to reflect how uncertainty compounds over time. At one day, realized volatility is relatively contained, so the 90% interval spans roughly 24 points (314–338), which corresponds to a typical daily move range assuming moderate volatility. By one week, the interval widens to 47 points (305–352), reflecting the accumulation of daily randomness across five trading sessions. At one month, the interval expands to 95 points (285–380), acknowledging that over roughly 20 trading days, both trend and volatility compounding can drive substantial deviation from the starting point. These widths are broadly consistent with a log-normal price process with annualized volatility in the range of 15–20%.

Specific risks that could push outcomes outside these intervals include unexpected macroeconomic data releases — such as a surprise inflation print, a central bank pivot, or a major geopolitical escalation — any of which could produce gap moves exceeding the stated bounds within a single day. Earnings announcements, if this is an individual equity, or sector-specific regulatory news could similarly cause discontinuous jumps. On the downside, a broader risk-off episode or liquidity event could push prices well below 285 at the one-month horizon.

The tail risks are asymmetric in character. Sharp downside moves tend to be faster and more correlated across assets, meaning the lower bound of the one-month interval may be more likely to be breached than the upper bound in a stress scenario. Conversely, a sustained momentum rally or short-squeeze dynamic could blow through the upper bound more gradually but persistently. Both tails are plausible if conditions shift materially from what was observable at the time of the forecast.
